chapter: Cass Carr, Crawley, Burnet and Cootie Williams
title: Wilton Crawley's clarinet and contortion act
summary: Crawley was a Keith-circuit vaudeville single who took his clarinet apart, balanced a lit kerosene lamp and played upside down.

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: Speaking of odd instruments, like the musical saw, there was a musician that you got hooked up with (for a recording date anyway) by the name of Wilton Crawley.
Yeah, but that was not no weird instrument he had. He was a clarinet player. A clarinet is a legitimate instrument.
But maybe it was perhaps the way he...
Oh, the way he was playing it.
Maybe you could tell us about Crawley and about his successful act and so on.

Wilton Crawley, let me see. I couldn't put him down as a clarinet player. I couldn't call him a clarinet player, because the man had more to offer than clarinet players have to offer. Because the man was an acrobat, he was a contortionist, he sang, and he wrote music... Well, he did just about it all. He had his own style of playing, and I wouldn't say that it was bad. But I wouldn't say it was good either. But he had his own style of playing.
And he was a very big act on the B.F. Keith Circuit. That was the top vaudeville circuit at that time. And he was a big act on the B.F. Keith Circuit. He could come out

with that clarinet, and play it, and start taking it apart from the lowest joint, take that off, and then he'd take the middle joint off and be playing half the clarinet, and then he would take that joint off, and it would leave him playing nothing but the mouthpiece -- and he would still be playing. And then he would go to the end of the stage, and look into the wings, and he would come back with a lamp on his head, a kerosene lamp -- and it would be lit. He'd come in with this lamp on his head, he's still playing this mouthpiece...
So it was a live flame.

Yeah. And he'd still be playing his clarinet, you know. So he's putting the clarinet back together again now. Because he'd got down to the mouthpiece. Now he's putting it back together again, and he's playing it, and he's balancing this kerosene lamp on his head, and he's going into all kind of contortions, acts and things. So it ends up where the clarinet is...he gets the clarinet back together, he's playing it, gets the clarinet back together, the lamp is on his head, and I don't know how he does it, but he ended up being on his head, too, playing the clarinet and balancing the lamp. I mean, it was a wonderful act! You wouldn't believe it. I don't know how he did it. But it made a lot of big money.
And he was on stage just by himself.
He was by himself, yeah. He was a single.
And he wrote his own music?
Yeah, he wrote his own music.
And then the pit band would play it.

Well, I don't say... I mean, he would write his numbers. But I don't say he arranged the music for the orchestra. I don't think he was an arranger. But I mean, he could scratch out a melody, you know. Oh, he was very entertaining to look at, but I could do without listening to him. Strike that out.
